common_name: Daniel Weeks Ginger Lily (Golden Butterfly Ginger)

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions into rich, well-drained beds once the soil has warmed after last frost; this hybrid is one of the more cold-tolerant gingers and can be left in the ground further north than most.

directions: Grow in bright filtered light with several hours of morning sun to encourage the long spikes of golden-yellow, honeysuckle-scented flowers that open from midsummer clear through the first frost. Keep the root zone evenly moist and feed monthly during the growing season to sustain the tall, arching canes. Where winters dip below the mid-teens, cut stalks back after frost and blanket the crown with a thick mulch layer to protect the rhizomes.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Pink V Ginger Lily (Peachy-Pink Butterfly Ginger)

planting.note: Plant divisions in warm, humus-rich soil after the last frost; this Tom Wood hybrid stays a manageable size, making it a good fit for smaller Gulf Coast borders and large containers.

directions: Site this compact hybrid where it gets dappled shade through the heat of the day, since strong afternoon sun can scorch the foliage before the peachy-pink flower cones appear in late summer and fall. Keep soil consistently damp and mulch well to hold moisture between waterings. Divide congested clumps every two to three years in spring to keep flowering strong and to share starts with other gardeners.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Disney Scarlet Ginger Lily (Orange-Red Butterfly Ginger)

planting.note: Set divisions out after the soil has warmed in spring, giving this tall selection several hours of direct sun daily to keep its naturally upright canes from leaning.

directions: Give this selection more direct sun than most Hedychium coccineum forms, since four to five hours of light strengthens the stems and boosts flowering of the fragrant, brilliant orange-red spikes. The reddish-backed, glossy foliage stays notably erect rather than flopping, so it works well as a dramatic accent behind lower plantings. Keep the soil rich and evenly moist through summer, and mulch the crowns heavily once cold weather cuts the top growth back.

common_name: Stephen Dwarf Ginger Lily (Butterscotch Butterfly Ginger)

planting.note: Tuck divisions of this compact Himalayan selection into the front or middle of a shaded border after last frost, where its narrow foliage and modest size fit spaces too small for taller ginger lilies.

directions: This dwarf selection, collected in Nepal, stays under three and a half feet tall with slender leaves and repeat flushes of butterscotch-yellow flowers accented by orange anthers from midsummer into early fall. Grow it in part shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, and avoid crowding it behind larger gingers where it can be shaded out. Because of its smaller stature, it also performs well in a large patio container that can be moved to shelter in a cold snap.

common_name: CP Raffill Ginger Lily (Early Orange Butterfly Ginger)

planting.note: Plant divisions in fertile, moisture-retentive soil after the last frost; this early-flowering selection often begins blooming ahead of other ginger lilies, so give it a full growing season head start where summers are short.

directions: Named for its Kew Gardens breeder, this award-winning selection produces unusually large, richly colored orange flower heads that open earlier in summer than most Hedychium coccineum forms. Site it in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade, and keep the soil evenly moist through the growing season to support the sturdy clumps and their oversized bloom spikes. Divide crowded clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigorous flowering and propagate new plants.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
